analysis.one_liner: Restores canceled Arctic Refuge oil leases, blocks their future cancellation, and limits environmental review and lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 214-199 on May 1, 2024, but the Senate never voted on it before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo Biden administration actions that paused or canceled oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and parts of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. It would require the Interior Department to reissue six canceled lease tracts to the companies that bid on them, hold a second lease sale, declare the old environmental paperwork sufficient under laws like the Endangered Species Act, and strip courts of the power to review the program's approvals. It also bars the President and Interior from canceling leases in the future.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that bid on Arctic Refuge leases in January 2021 would get their canceled leases back on the original terms, and future leaseholders would gain security because the government could not cancel their leases. Supporters also argued Alaska communities and state revenue would benefit from development.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies holding Arctic Refuge lease bids

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies any presidential or Interior Department order that pauses leasing in the refuge's 1002 Area and ratifies every permit, biological opinion, and approval issued for the Coastal Plain leasing program.
Requires Interior, within 30 days of enactment, to accept the bids from the January 6, 2021 lease sale and reissue leases for six tracts whose leases the administration canceled.
Requires a second lease sale in the refuge by December 22, 2024, and bars the President and Interior from canceling future leases unless the lessee violates lease terms.

Withdraws the draft supplemental environmental impact statement for the leasing program, voids the final rule protecting the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, and nullifies Section 4 of Executive Order 13990 and Secretarial Order 3401.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental and legal costs: the reissued leases would be declared, by statute, to satisfy the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and other laws without any new review, and courts would be barred from hearing challenges to the program's approvals. Development would proceed in a refuge whose coastal plain is calving ground for the Porcupine caribou herd and central to Gwich'in subsistence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public lands and anyone seeking to sue

drawbacks.text: The bill declares the reissued leases to satisfy the Endangered Species Act, NEPA, the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act as they existed at the time, meaning no new environmental analysis before drilling rights are granted.

It strips courts of jurisdiction over any approval under the leasing program, including lawsuits already pending at enactment; the only challenges allowed go to a single court about the scope of that provision itself, and leaseholders get their own special petition process if an agency delays.
It locks in the leases by prohibiting the President or Interior from canceling them, taking that decision away from future administrations regardless of what new information emerges.

It nullifies the Bureau of Land Management's management rule for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and requires an act of Congress before any new protected Special Areas can be designated there, reversing land-use protections on millions of acres of public land.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' strongest argument is that Congress itself ordered this leasing program in the 2017 tax law and the administration then declined to carry it out, so the bill simply enforces a mandate Congress wrote [S5]. The cost side is substantial: the bill does not just restart leasing, it forecloses environmental review, cancels petroleum-reserve protections, and removes the public's ability to challenge the program in court. The judicial-stripping and statutory environmental waivers go well beyond what enforcing the original mandate would require.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 214-199 on May 1, 2024, but the Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the next day and it died there without ever getting a vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a 24-17 vote on December 6, 2023, and reported it amended on April 15, 2024.
On May 1, 2024, Democrats moved to recommit the bill to committee; the motion failed 201-211, with all 201 voting Democrats in favor and all 211 voting Republicans opposed.
The House passed the bill 214-199 with 2 present: 209 of the 217 voting Republicans and 5 of the 212 voting Democrats voted yes.
The Senate received the bill on May 2, 2024, referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and took no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in the Senate, the lease cancellations and petroleum-reserve protections it targeted stayed in place, and the oil companies hoping to recover their Arctic Refuge leases through legislation got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of Arctic drilling kept current policy

for.name: Pete Stauber
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through committee and floor consideration.

for.name: 209 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage; only 1 voting Republican voted no.

for.name: Bruce Westerman
for.what_they_did: Chaired the markup that ordered the bill reported 24-17 and reported it to the floor.

against.name: 198 of 216 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; 198 of 212 voting Democrats opposed, and all 201 voting Democrats backed sending the bill back to committee.

against.name: Kathy Castor
against.role: House Democratic deputy leader / energy policy leader
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee, a last chance to change it before the final vote; the motion failed 201-211.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and took no action, so the Senate never voted on it.

against.name: President Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: His administration canceled the January 2021 Arctic Refuge leases, issued the petroleum reserve rule, and paused leasing — the actions this bill was written to overturn — and opposed its approach.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 209 of 217 voting Republicans yes versus 5 of 212 voting Democrats; the motion to recommit was 201-211 down party lines, with every voting Democrat for it and every voting Republican against.

industries.industry: Oil and gas industry (Arctic leaseholders and Alaska producers)
industries.note: The bill would hand the companies their canceled leases back on original terms, permanently bar lease cancellation, and shield every program approval from court challenge, locking in their drilling rights with no environmental re-review. The public bears the environmental risk while losing its day in court.
